# 9.1 $k$-means {background-color="#16181A" style="color:#F7F6F3"}

## The objective

Partition observations into $k$ clusters minimising within-cluster sum of squares:

$$\min_{C_1,\dots,C_k} \sum_{j=1}^{k} \sum_{i \in C_j} \|x_i - \mu_j\|^2, \qquad
\mu_j = \frac{1}{|C_j|}\sum_{i\in C_j} x_i$$

::: {.muted}
The problem is **NP-hard**.
:::

## Lloyd's algorithm

Two steps, each weakly decreasing the objective:

::: {.tight}
1. **Assign:** $c_i \leftarrow \arg\min_j \|x_i - \mu_j\|^2$
2. **Update:** $\mu_j \leftarrow$ mean of points assigned to $j$
:::

Step 2 is optimal given assignments (differentiate in $\mu_j$, set to zero); step 1 is optimal given
centroids.

## Why it terminates — and where

The objective decreases monotonically and there are finitely many partitions, so the algorithm
terminates — **at a local minimum**.

::: {.warn}
Run it many times from different starts (`n_init`), or use **k-means++**, which seeds centroids with
probability proportional to squared distance from the nearest existing centroid and gives an
$O(\log k)$-competitive guarantee in expectation.
:::

## What the Euclidean objective assumes

Because clusters are defined by nearest-centroid, the decision boundaries are the perpendicular
bisectors between centroids — a **Voronoi tessellation**.

::: {.check}
This *forces* convex, roughly spherical, similarly-sized clusters. Elongated or nested structures
will be cut incorrectly **no matter how well you optimise.**
:::

::: {.muted}
If that assumption is wrong: a Gaussian mixture (covariance structure, soft assignments via EM), or
DBSCAN / spectral clustering for non-convex shapes.
:::

# 9.2 Hierarchical clustering {background-color="#16181A" style="color:#F7F6F3"}

## Linkage defines "closest"

Build a dendrogram bottom-up, merging the two closest clusters at each step.

| Linkage | $d(A,B)$ | Behaviour |
|---|---|---|
| Single | $\min_{a,b}\|a-b\|$ | Chaining; elongated shapes; unstable |
| Complete | $\max_{a,b}\|a-b\|$ | Compact, similar-diameter clusters |
| Average | mean pairwise distance | Compromise; not invariant to monotone transforms |
| **Ward** | increase in within-cluster SS | Same criterion as $k$-means; the default to try |

## The trade

::: {.tight}
- **Advantage:** you need not fix $k$ in advance — the dendrogram shows structure at every resolution
- **Cost:** $O(n^2)$ memory
:::

# 9.3 Choosing $k$ {background-color="#16181A" style="color:#F7F6F3"}

## Elbow

Plot within-cluster SS against $k$. It **always** decreases, so look for a kink.

::: {.warn}
Often no kink exists. A single elbow plot is not evidence.
:::

## Silhouette

For observation $i$:

$$s_i = \frac{b_i - a_i}{\max(a_i,b_i)}$$

with $a_i$ the mean distance to its own cluster and $b_i$ to the nearest other cluster.

::: {.tight}
- near **1** — well clustered
- near **0** — on a boundary
- **negative** — probably misassigned
:::

Average over $i$, maximise over $k$.

## Gap statistic

Compare $\log W_k$ to its expectation under a null reference distribution — uniform over the data's
bounding box, or a PCA-aligned box. Choose the smallest $k$ where the gap exceeds the next $k$'s gap
minus one standard error.

::: {.check}
This one **can return $k=1$** — "no cluster structure". Which is why it is worth the extra effort:
it is the only one of the three that can tell you to stop.
:::

## Report at least two

::: {.warn}
**And report disagreement.** On the course spine — built from **four** country types — the
silhouette score on the country profiles peaks at **six**. The diagnostic is confidently wrong, on
data where we happen to know the answer.
:::

::: {.muted}
You will not have that luxury with real data. Which is the point of noticing it here.
:::

# 9.4 Representing text {background-color="#16181A" style="color:#F7F6F3"}

## Bag of words / TF-IDF

$$\mathrm{tf\text{-}idf}(t,d) = \underbrace{f_{t,d}}_{\text{term frequency}} \times
\underbrace{\log\frac{N}{1 + n_t}}_{\text{inverse document frequency}}$$

The idf factor downweights ubiquitous terms.

::: {.check}
The result is a very sparse, very high-dimensional matrix — exactly the $p \gg n$ setting of
Sessions 05 and 06, so **penalised regression is the natural supervised tool on top of it.**
:::

## What bag-of-words throws away

Word order, entirely.

> *"Inflation is not a concern"* and *"a concern is not inflation"* are **identical vectors**.

::: {.muted}
Two-word n-grams recover a little of the negation. Not all of it.
:::

## Dense embeddings

A model maps each document to $v_d \in \mathbb{R}^m$ (typically $m$ = 384 to 1024), trained so that
semantically similar texts have similar vectors. Similarity by cosine:

$$\cos(v_a, v_b) = \frac{v_a^\top v_b}{\|v_a\|\|v_b\|} \in [-1,1]$$

::: {.check}
Cosine ignores magnitude — which is what you want when documents differ in length.
:::

## Generated locally

You will generate embeddings **on your own machine** in the lab.

::: {.muted}
The corpus never leaves it. That is both a methodological and a governance point, and it is worth
saying out loud in a paper.
:::

## Do not assume sophistication is progress

**Dictionary methods** — counting terms from a pre-specified list — remain widely used in economics
precisely because they are **transparent and auditable**.

::: {.warn}
An embedding-based index that nobody can interrogate may be *less* useful for policy than a word
count anyone can check.
:::

# 9.5 Validity {background-color="#16181A" style="color:#F7F6F3"}

## Four questions about any text-derived measure

::: {.tight}
1. **Face validity** — read a random sample of high- and low-scoring documents. Do they look like
   what you claim to measure?
2. **Convergent validity** — does the index correlate with independent measures of the same
   construct?
3. **Predictive validity** — does it forecast something it should?
4. **Robustness** — does it survive changes in preprocessing, vocabulary and model?
:::

## On the first one

::: {.check}
**Do this. Actually read them.** It takes twenty minutes and it has killed more bad indices than any
statistic.
:::

## On the fourth

> If your finding depends on a stemming choice, **you do not have a finding.**

::: {.warn}
Also check your index against document length. An index that correlates strongly with word count is
a length detector with extra steps — and that is one line to test.
:::

# The lab {background-color="#16181A" style="color:#F7F6F3"}

## What you do

::: {.tight}
1. Cluster your angle's units; report **two** criteria for $k$ and any disagreement
2. Test stability under resampling — do units change cluster?
3. Build one text measure, normalised per thousand words, not raw counts
4. Run all four validity checks, including the length correlation
:::

::: {.warn}
Corpus composition drives raw counts. If more documents are published, term frequency rises with no
change in attention. **Normalise, and say how in the caption.**
:::

## The two-minute report

::: {.tight}
1. **What I did** — the representation, the normalisation, the model and version
2. **The number** — your index, and what it correlates with
3. **The catch** — say "our index of X", never "X"
:::

Full brief: [`02-lab/README.md`](02-lab/README.md)
:::
